docs.title: Introducing CUDA-Q Pulse: Python-native pulse programming with GPUs in the loop
docs.text:
Gates are the currency of quantum applications. But every quantum gate is a convenient abstraction, representing a shaped microwave or laser pulse executing across a control line with nanosecond precision. Calibration, quantum error correction (QEC), and device bring-up all happen at that deeper layer, and very often crafting and operating with those pulses requires GPU calculations to make fast decisions during quantum runtime.

Today we're releasing CUDA-Q Pulse (cudaq-pulse), an open-source pulse-level programming model and MLIR compiler. This new addition to the NVIDIA quantum platform allows users to write pulse programs in ordinary Python and call classical functions on a GPU, host, or FPGA in the middle of the experiment. It can work within explicit latency budgets, and simulate the whole loop involved in pulse programming with NVIDIA cuDensityMat before running it on quantum hardware.

docs.title: Why pulses, and why this release
docs.text:
Gate-level frameworks give algorithm developers a clean interface. But the work that makes a quantum processor (QPU) function, such as tuning a π pulse, tracking a drifting T1, echoing away crosstalk, or choosing an action before the next quantum error correction round, is written in terms of control lines, tones and waveforms. Until now that code has mostly lived in sequencer languages tied to one control system - making it hard to share or simulate.

The classical side of that loop is also becoming increasingly demanding. Adaptive calibration runs a Bayesian estimator between shots. Real-time QEC needs a decoder to answer before the next syndrome round. NVQLink gives QPUs access to GPUs with microsecond latency, and cudaq-realtime provides the runtime for those calls. CUDA-Q Pulse adds the programming model, a single Python source that describes the pulses, the measurements, and the classical calls between them, compiled to an open MLIR representation that any control system can utilize.

  • Python-native kernels

    @pulse.kernel functions are ordinary Python, with loops, comprehensions, *qudits, helpers, and direct calls. They trace to a typed MLIR pulse dialect in milliseconds.

  • Real-time classical calls

    @pulse.classical declares a function the pulse program calls during quantum runtime, with a typed data layout and a latency budget. The scheduler treats it like any other operation.

  • CPU and GPU simulation

    The same kernel runs on a NumPy reference simulator or lowers through an operator dialect to NVIDIA cuDensityMat, so you can run full pulse routines against a physics model of a quantum system, including a 17-qubit surface-code processor from the literature.

  • Open, hardware-agnostic IR

    Pulses, waits, syncs, loops, and measurement-conditioned branches compile to MLIR and, through export_to_controller(), to a versioned program that control-system vendors can lower to their own sequencers, with no dependency on cudaq-realtime.

CUDA-Q Pulse ships as pip-installable wheels covering Python 3.12 through free-threaded Python 3.14t, with CUDA 12 and CUDA 13 GPU simulation on Linux through the [cu12] and [cu13] extras.

Experimental release

CUDA-Q Pulse is currently an experimental, standalone release that's separate from the CUDA-Q product. APIs may change between versions as we work with the community. We want your feedback in GitHub issues.

docs.title: A pulse kernel is simple Python
docs.text:
A kernel works with a small set of physical resources. Lines carry signals to and from a qubit, and tones hold the frequency and phase that a line operates at. Inside the kernel, a handful of operations do the work: drive, readout, wait, sync, and phase and frequency updates on tones. Waveforms like gaussian, drag, and square are values you can build and pass to other functions - as shown in the below example.

import cudaq_pulse as pulse


@pulse.kernel
def rabi(qudit, amplitude: float):
    d = get_drive_line(qudit)     # the line that drives the qudit
    r = get_readout_line(qudit)   # the line that reads it out
    drive(d, gaussian(duration=32 * pulse.ns, amplitude=amplitude, sigma=8 * pulse.ns))
    sync(d, r)                    # start the readout after the drive pulse ends
    return readout(r, square(300 * pulse.ns, 0.05))


qs = pulse.quantum_system("transmon_surface17")
q = qs.qudits[0]

# Sweep the drive amplitude. A float argument stays symbolic, so this compiles once.
for amplitude in [0.04, 0.1, 0.16]:
    result = pulse.simulate(rabi, q, amplitude)
    p1 = result.level_population(1)   # excited-state population: 0.15, 0.65, 0.96

Calling rabi(q, 0.16) is an ordinary Python call. The first call traces the function's bytecode into the Pulse MLIR dialect, compiles it, and runs it on the selected quantum system. Each specialization is cached, so repeat calls skip compilation.

We spent much of this release making kernels read like standard Python. Comprehensions, generator expressions, starred unpacking, *qudits parameters, methods, and decorated helpers all trace. Here's a Ramsey sequence across every qubit on a 17-qubit device:

@pulse.kernel
def parallel_ramsey(qudits, tau: float):
    for q in qudits:
        d = get_drive_line(q)
        x90 = d.get_calibration(pulse.gates.X90)   # this line's calibrated π/2 pulse
        drive(d, x90)
        wait(d, tau * pulse.ns)                    # free evolution for tau
        drive(d, x90)

scheduled = parallel_ramsey.lower(qs.qudits[0:17], 200.0)   # compile and schedule all 17

When something can't trace, the error names your file and line and tells you what to write instead. A python -m cudaq_pulse.doctor --setup-editor command and a mypy plugin clear editor warnings on bare kernel operations such as drive and readout, and the command writes that configuration for you when you confirm.

docs.title: Calling a GPU in the middle of an experiment
docs.text:
Many of the most valuable control loops need a classical answer during the middle of an experiment. A decoder may need to report whether a syndrome indicated an error, or an estimator may need to pick the next wait from what was just measured. CUDA-Q Pulse adds a classical dialect so a pulse program can call a function on the controller or a GPU during quantum runtime and use the answer immediately.

import cudaq_pulse as pulse

# A function that runs on a GPU while the qubits wait. Its answer comes back
# within 3.8 us of the request. In simulation, this Python body gives the answer.
@pulse.classical(link="gpu", max_latency_ns=3_800)
def decode(syndrome: pulse.Bits) -> bool:
    return bool(syndrome[0])

@pulse.kernel
def feedback_and_adapt(q):
    d = get_drive_line(q)
    r = get_readout_line(q)
    pi_pulse = d.get_calibration(pulse.gates.X)
    outcome = readout(r, square(300 * pulse.ns, 0.05))

    # Ask the decoder, waiting at most 4 us. If it's late, use the raw outcome.
    request = decode.submit([outcome])
    in_time, flip = request.result(timeout=4 * pulse.us)
    correct = flip if in_time else outcome
    sync(d, r)
    if correct:
        drive(d, pi_pulse)

# The control system reaches the GPU over a link named "gpu" (NVQLink).
control_system = pulse.ControlSystem(links={"gpu": pulse.Link(feedback_ns=50)})
qs = pulse.quantum_system("transmon_surface17")
compiled = pulse.compile(feedback_and_adapt, control_system=control_system)
scheduled = compiled.lower(qs.qudits[0])
report = scheduled.classical_report()   # when each answer is due: decode, slack 0 ns

The decoder's 3.8 µs latency follows FPGA-GPU-FPGA round trips over NVQLink, which measure 2.9–3.8 µs on an RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell host (details).

Figure 1. One shot with real-time calls. The decoder's answer gates a conditional pulse, as in feedback_and_adapt, and an estimator sets a wait whose length is known only at runtime, as described in the calibration section below.

There are three points to note about this example:

  • The call is a contract. @pulse.classical records which function to call, the exact data layout going in and out, and a latency budget. That's everything a control system needs to schedule the call and everything a GPU service needs to answer it.
  • Late answers are handled explicitly. .result(timeout=...) returns an in-time flag along with the value, so a kernel can fall back instead of stalling the QPU.
  • Runtime values stay schedulable. A wait whose length comes from an estimator, like the adaptive T1 tracker's below, carries bounds, so the scheduler can still reason about timing across lines.

Underneath, this rests on mid-circuit measurement and control flow that survive from the Python trace, through region-aware scheduling, into our simulators. In simulation the Python body of each classical function runs. On hardware, the same declaration is what a control-system backend implements, whether the function runs on the controller's FPGA or on a GPU over NVQLink. It's also the hook for plugging CUDA-Q QEC decoders into GPU-in-the-loop syndrome decoding.

Where the function body runs How it's declared What fits in the budget Python, in simulation any @pulse.classical function Develop and test the full loop against a simulated quantum system Controller FPGA a link to the controller, such as link="controller" Sub-microsecond updates, such as an estimator NVIDIA GPU over NVQLink a link to the GPU, such as link="gpu" Microsecond-scale work such as QEC decoding and heavier estimators

In this release, classical calls run end to end in simulation. Lowering them onto specific controllers and NVQLink transports will be available in a future release.

docs.title: Real-time decoding with a deadline
docs.text:
QEC has demanding timing requirements. The 17-qubit processor modeled below ran its distance-3 surface-code cycle in 1.1 µs, then ran decoding, finally applying corrections in post-processing (Krinner et al.). In real-time operation however, a decoder has to produce answer while the qubits wait, and the program needs a plan for the shots when the decoder is late or unable to respond.

Fast implementations of popular decoders are defined in CUDA-Q QEC and a pulse program can call them as a CUDA-Q kernel does: pulse.classical takes CUDA-Q QEC's own real-time functions, cudaq_qec.qec.enqueue_syndromes and get_corrections, with a link and a latency budget. On hardware, their requests are the messages of CUDA-Q QEC's decoding server; in simulation, the decoder you configured answers them. As an example, here's one round of a distance-3 repetition code with CUDA-Q QEC's GPU decoder, nv-qldpc-decoder (belief propagation with ordered-statistics post-processing, BP+OSD). Note that reproducing this example requires a Linux system running Python 3.12 or 3.13 and connected to an NVIDIA GPU.

import cudaq_qec
import numpy as np

import cudaq_pulse as pulse

# Set up decoder 0 in CUDA-Q QEC: BP+OSD on the GPU for a distance-3
# repetition code (2 syndrome bits in, 1 correction bit per data qubit out).
cudaq_qec.configure_decoders_from_str("""
decoders:
  - id: 0
    type: nv-qldpc-decoder
    block_size: 3
    syndrome_size: 2
    H_sparse: [0, 1, -1, 1, 2, -1]
    O_sparse: [0, -1, 1, -1, 2, -1]
    D_sparse: [0, -1, 1, -1]
    decoder_custom_args:
      error_rate_vec: [0.1, 0.1, 0.1]
      use_sparsity: true
      max_iterations: 50
      use_osd: true
      osd_method: 3
      osd_order: 7
""")

# CUDA-Q QEC's real-time calls, sent to the decoder over the GPU link.
# Corrections come back in about 62 us, and 75 us at worst.
enqueue_syndromes = pulse.classical(cudaq_qec.qec.enqueue_syndromes, link="gpu")
get_corrections = pulse.classical(cudaq_qec.qec.get_corrections, link="gpu",
                                  nominal_latency_ns=62_000, max_latency_ns=75_000)

@pulse.kernel
def qec_round(data, ancillas, deadline_ns: int):
    # ... syndrome-extraction pulses on data and ancillas go here ...
    # Read out the two ancillas to get the syndrome.
    s0 = readout(get_readout_line(ancillas[0]), square(400 * pulse.ns, 0.05))
    s1 = readout(get_readout_line(ancillas[1]), square(400 * pulse.ns, 0.05))

    # Send the syndrome to decoder 0 (round 0), then wait for its
    # 3 correction bits, but no longer than the deadline.
    enqueue_syndromes.submit(0, [s0, s1], 0)
    request = get_corrections.submit(0, 3, False)
    in_time, fix = request.result(timeout=deadline_ns * pulse.ns)

    # If the decoder is late, use a lookup table on the controller instead.
    table = [s0 and not s1, s0 and s1, s1 and not s0]
    for i in range(3):
        flip = fix[i] if in_time else table[i]
        if flip:
            drive(get_drive_line(data[i]), square(20 * pulse.ns, np.pi / 20))   # π pulse

The kernel sends the syndrome, asks for corrections with a deadline, and keeps a lookup table on the controller for shots where the answer is late. The deadline is a kernel parameter, so you can trade waiting against falling back without editing the program. Compiling checks the timing before anything runs:

qs = pulse.quantum_system("transmon_lattice:5")   # five transmons
data = qs.qudits[0:3]
ancillas = qs.qudits[3:5]

control_system = pulse.ControlSystem(links={"gpu": pulse.Link(feedback_ns=50)})
compiled = pulse.compile(qec_round, quantum_system=qs, control_system=control_system)
scheduled = compiled.lower(data, ancillas, 80_000)   # deadline: 80 us
report = scheduled.classical_report()   # get_corrections is due at 80.5 us

In a simulation that starts from the state syndrome extraction leaves, every single-qubit error is corrected on the right qubit, by the decoder when it answers in time and by the table when it doesn't. examples/27_realtime_decoding.py runs it end to end.

Figure 2. One round of qec_round. The correction pulse plays from the decoder's answer if it arrives by the deadline, or from the controller's lookup table if it doesn't.

The same messages also went to a real decoder. On a workstation with an NVIDIA RTX A6000 GPU, the CUDA-QX decoding server ran with cudaq-realtime, serving the same nv-qldpc-decoder configuration on the GPU, and CUDA-Q Pulse's syndrome messages connected to it with no changes. Over 5,000 shots, the server's corrections matched the local emulation exactly, and shots whose answer came back after the deadline took the fallback table. From sending the syndrome to receiving the correction, round trips took about 62 µs typically and 75 µs at the 99.9th percentile, the latency budget in the code above. Replaying those round trips in CUDA-Q Pulse's emulator, a deadline at the median sends 45% of shots to the fallback table, one at the 99th percentile 0.75%, and one at the 99.9th percentile 0.06%.

Those numbers aren't a QPU's latency, and they are different from the 2.9–3.8 µs NVQLink round trips above. The test was host-to-GPU loopback: a process on the same machine sent each request over UDP through the operating system's network stack, and the server launched the decoder from the host. On NVQLink, requests travel from the controller's FPGA to the GPU without passing through the host's operating system. Loopback shows that the messages, corrections, and fallback logic are right; the hardware path brings the round trip down to a few syndrome rounds.

docs.title: Calibration as one program
docs.text:
Calibration is where real-time classical control pays off first. Researchers track fluctuating qubit relaxation in real time with a Bayesian estimator (Berritta et al., Phys. Rev. X 16, 011025 (2026)) and calibrate and benchmark superconducting qubits at millisecond scale (Marciniak et al., arXiv:2602.11912). Both experiments run their estimators on the controller's FPGA, because the feedback loop has to close in microseconds.

We implemented that protocol end to end in CUDA-Q Pulse. Characterization, estimation, parameter update, and pulse regeneration are a single program, with the estimators declared on the controller link.

Here's the core of the adaptive T1 tracker. Each shot's wait comes from the previous shot's estimate, and the estimator has 500 ns to answer.

import cudaq_pulse as pulse
from cudaq_pulse.classical import calibration as cal

# Berritta et al.'s Bayesian update of the T1 estimate (a gamma posterior over
# 1/T1, with parameters shape and rate), which also picks the next wait.
# It runs on the controller, within 500 ns.
@pulse.classical(link="controller", max_latency_ns=500)
def update_t1(bit: pulse.Bits, shape: float, rate: float,
              wait_ns: float) -> tuple[float, float, float]:
    shape, rate = cal.adaptive_t1_update(shape, rate, bit[0], wait_ns,
                                         error_1to0=0.11, error_0to1=0.14)
    next_wait_ns = cal.adaptive_t1_wait(shape, rate)
    next_wait_ns = min(max(next_wait_ns, 100.0), 200_000.0)   # keep it in 100 ns to 200 us
    return shape, rate, next_wait_ns

@pulse.kernel
def track_t1(q, shots_count: int, shape: float, rate: float, wait_ns: float):
    d = get_drive_line(q)
    r = get_readout_line(q)
    pi_pulse = d.get_calibration(pulse.gates.X)
    for shot in range(shots_count):     # every shot adapts, inside one kernel
        drive(d, pi_pulse)              # excite, then let it decay for wait_ns
        wait(d, wait_ns * pulse.ns, bounds=(100 * pulse.ns, 200 * pulse.us))
        sync(d, r)
        outcome = readout(r, square(300 * pulse.ns, 0.05))
        # The controller updates the estimate and picks the next wait.
        shape, rate, wait_ns = update_t1.submit([outcome], shape, rate, wait_ns).result()
        sync(d, r)
        if outcome:
            drive(d, pi_pulse)          # active reset
Figure 3. Fifty adaptive shots in one kernel. The estimator on the controller updates its posterior after each readout and picks the next wait. The shot lengths on the right are schematic, not data.

We checked the tracker against the paper in simulation. On a model qubit with a T1 of 160 µs and the paper's assignment errors, 400 simulated runs of 50 adaptive shots gave a median estimate of 155 µs, with 68% of runs between 123 and 195 µs. Berritta et al. report 159 µs, with a 68% interval of 131 to 202 µs, on their processor.

Figure 4. The T1 estimate after each of 50 adaptive shots, in simulation. The uncertainty of a single run's estimate narrows from the starting guess to around the model's true T1. On the right, the final estimates of 400 runs beside Berritta et al.'s result.

The same structure covers the rest of the protocol; with another estimator or other pulses, the compiler schedules the new loop. Because the estimator is ordinary Python in simulation, you can develop and test it against a simulated quantum system before you lower it to a controller.

docs.title: A 17-qubit quantum system on GPUs
docs.text:
To test programs like these without access to a physical QPU, CUDA-Q Pulse includes a physics model of the 17-qubit superconducting processor used to demonstrate repeated error correction in a distance-3 surface code (Krinner et al., Nature 605, 669 (2022)). The model accounts for exchange coupling, residual ZZ, thermal populations, and Hahn-echo dephasing, and it exposes fitted CZ parameters for all 24 coupled pairs. Flux pulses aren't simulated yet, so a program schedules each CZ as its calibrated time slot.

Figure 5. The transmon_surface17 quantum system. Pulse programs lower through the QOp operator dialect to cuDensityMat for GPU time evolution.

Selecting the quantum system requires only a single line of code, as used by most examples in this post:

import cudaq_pulse as pulse

qs = pulse.quantum_system("transmon_surface17")

When a kernel is simulated with backend="gpu", the compiler lowers the Pulse dialect into Hamiltonian and Lindblad terms in the QOp dialect and maps those to NVIDIA cuDensityMat. The pulse program you simulate is the same one you'd hand to a control system.

docs.title: Compiles fast enough for QEC-scale programs
docs.text:
A pulse compiler for fault-tolerant systems has to keep up with large codes. The MLIR compiler in CUDA-Q Pulse handles them comfortably:

Program (one synthetic syndrome-extraction cycle) Size Compile time Peak memory Distance-11 rotated surface code 241 qubits, 2,401 pulse operations 31 ms 39 MB Distance-21 rotated surface code 881 qubits, 9,201 pulse operations 120 ms 45 MB Distance-31 rotated surface code 1,921 qubits, 20,401 pulse operations 266 ms 53 MB Distance-51 rotated surface code 5,201 qubits, 56,001 pulse operations 790 ms 88 MB [[144,12,12]] bivariate bicycle (gross) code † 288 qubits, 4,320 pulse operations 54 ms 41 MB

† The gross-code benchmark ships in v0.1.1; the other rows reproduce with v0.1.0's benchmarks/simulation/qec_scaling.py.

Each surface-code row comes from benchmarks/simulation/qec_scaling.py --distances D --repeats 5, run in its own process for each distance, without optimization passes, on an x86-64 Linux workstation (Python 3.12 and the v0.1.0 wheels, in the manylinux container the wheels are built in). The compile time is the median of five compiles, and the peak memory is that of the whole Python process; the repository's performance notes give the host, the version, and the run-to-run spread for distance 31.

docs.title: Under the hood
docs.text:
Figure 6. One compiled program, three destinations.

The @pulse.kernel decorator captures the function's CPython bytecode. Tracing writes each operation into a compact packed buffer, which crosses into C++ in a single zero-copy call and becomes an in-memory MLIR module in the Pulse dialect. From there, MLIR passes verify the program, apply virtual-Z, fuse adjacent pulses, and schedule every operation as late as possible while respecting syncs and control-flow regions.

The scheduled program can be directed to one of three endpoints:

  • Simulation: the NumPy reference on any CPU, or Pulse → QOp → cuDensityMat on GPUs, for quantum systems like the 17-qubit one above.
  • Control systems: a vendor backend takes the program from export_to_controller() (pulses, waits, syncs, loops, and measurement-conditioned branches) and emits code for its own sequencers. CUDA-Q Pulse doesn't depend on cudaq-realtime, so backends can start with the pulse layer alone.
  • Real-time classical functions: @pulse.classical calls become first-class operations in the IR, with their data layout and deadline attached.

Each dialect performs a round-trip through parse and print, so MLIR from CUDA-Q Pulse is an artifact you can inspect and hand to another toolchain. Control-system teams that only need the compiler can run the dialects and passes on MLIR files with the cudaq-pulse-opt driver, which comes with the package.

docs.title: Get started
docs.text:
To work with CUDA-Q Pulse, install from PyPI and run the examples:

pip install cudaq-pulse            # compiler and CPU simulation (Linux, macOS)
pip install "cudaq-pulse[cu13]"    # plus GPU simulation with CUDA 13 (or [cu12])
python -m cudaq_pulse.doctor       # what's installed, and whether GPU simulation works
  • Explore the code. The CUDA-Q Pulse repository has numbered examples that run from a single-qubit Rabi experiment to GHZ state preparation.
  • Build a backend. If you build control systems, the controller export is the integration point. Open an issue on GitHub and tell us about your sequencer.
  • Learn how to use CUDA-Q Pulse in real-time workflows by leveraging cudaq-realtime and NVQLink to deliver microsecond GPU calls to the controller.

docs.title: QEC decoding comes online with the CUDA-Q QEC Decoding Server
docs.text:
Most quantum error correction (QEC) decoding today happens offline: sample a memory experiment, decode the shots, plot a logical error rate. A fault-tolerant QPU needs decoding as an online service instead. That service runs next to the controller for the life of the machine, takes syndromes as they arrive, and answers before the next round needs the result.

Today we're releasing CUDA-Q QEC 0.9 with the CUDA-Q QEC Decoding Server: an open-source reference application for online decoding. The Decoding Server ships in the cudaq-decoding container that anyone can download, experiment with, and deploy to a realtime host connected to a real or emulated QPU controller. Describe your decoders in one YAML file, start the server, and get corrections back over NVQLink RoCE or plain UDP. You can try it today with no hardware at all, by replaying recorded or simulated shots through the same server you'll later connect to your QPU.

Figure 1. The CUDA-Q QEC Decoding Server takes syndromes from a controller or the playback emulator, routes them through a decoding task graph, and returns corrections and logical results over the same link.

In this post we walk through the Decoding Server and its container, the wire format a controller uses to speak to it, how to test it without a QPU, and the task graphs and block-parallel scheduling that let it keep up with long streams of QEC syndrome extraction rounds (SERs).

docs.title: QEC decoding needs to be online
docs.text:
QEC decoding is the most demanding classical workload running within the Logical QPU. It is a single-user, real-time inference task with a deadline set by the logical clock rate of the QPU, and it runs for as long as the QPU is computing.

The QPU control system streams SERs to the decoder, and these form a queue. The SER rate depends on the QPU: about 1 kHz for trapped-ion and neutral-atom QPUs, and up to about 1 MHz for superconducting and spin-qubit QPUs.The decoder must process all of the syndrome data to keep a record of the current state of the QPU. The program reads from that record at feedforward events, such as applying a T gate, where the next operation depends on a logical measurement result.

There are three requirements for QEC decoding:

  1. Throughput is the rate at which SERs are retired from the queue. At each feedforward event (typically a non-Clifford gate), a throughput deficit leads to exponential growth in the SER backlog (Terhal 2015). This is critical: the decoder must keep up, or the logical instruction rate decays exponentially. This is often referred to as "the backlog problem." Riverlane, UCL and the University of Sheffield showed that parallel-window decoding can avoid the backlog problem by decoding windows of SERs in parallel, so throughput can grow with the number of independent decoders.
  2. Reaction time is the time the QPU spends waiting for a logical measurement result at a feedforward event. This is important because it is the inverse of the QPU's clock speed. Quantum Machines derived controller-decoder requirements by implementing Shor's algorithm with surface code, and found that the closed-loop latency must stay within tens of microseconds (Kurman et al. 2024). It is natural to count reaction time in SERs, because the logical qubits keep running SERs while they wait: tens of microseconds is tens of SERs on a 1 MHz QPU, and a few milliseconds is a few SERs on a 1 kHz QPU. Because the QPU waits on each result, decoder tail latency matters, not just the average: rare hard cases can dominate runtime even when average behavior is good.
  3. Accuracy is how often the decoder infers the correct logical correction. Decoding is a degenerate inference problem, and we may trade off throughput and reaction time against accuracy. This is important because accuracy contributes to the logical error rate.

Throughput and reaction time can be decoupled through pipelining and parallelism, as in a superscalar processor, where the number of instructions retired per second is not simply the inverse of the time to execute one instruction. For example, Google's below-threshold demonstration on their Willow QPU decoded a distance-5 surface code in real time at a 1.1 µs cycle time, with an average decoder latency of 63 µs (Google Quantum AI 2024), so about 57 SERs were in flight at once. How hard each requirement is depends on the SER rate. On a 1 kHz QPU, a decoder with Willow's latency would finish each SER before the next one arrived, so throughput is easy to meet and reaction time sets the pace of the logical clock. On a 1 MHz QPU, the decoder needs many SERs in flight to keep up, and reaction time still has to stay within tens of SERs. Below, we look at throughput and tail latency for block-parallel decoding through two examples: Relay BP for a 1 kHz QPU, and PyMatching for faster ones.

docs.title: Introducing the CUDA-Q QEC Decoding Server
docs.text:
CUDA-Q QEC 0.6 put GPU-accelerated decoders inside the control loop through cudaq-realtime. That release gave every NVQLink system a path to real-time decoding, but each user still had to write their own C++ to load decoders, manage buffers, and answer the controller.

The Decoding Server, released in CUDA-Q QEC 0.9, provides a reference implementation of that plumbing, so users can build on working code instead of reinventing it. The Decoding Server is one process, configured by one file, that speaks one documented wire format. Control-system builders implement the wire format once. QEC researchers change decoders by editing the configuration file, or plug in their own. QPU operators run the same container in the lab that they tested on a workstation.

The release ships the server as the cudaq-decoding container for x86 and arm64, with CUDA 12 and CUDA 13 variants. The image includes the decoding_server binary, its decoder plugins, nvq++, and worked examples. The source lives in the open-source CUDA-Q QEC repository, so you can rebuild it or extend it.

To try it out, start the container on the host that will do your decoding:

export DECODING_SERVER_IMAGE='nvcr.io/nvidia/quantum/cudaq-decoding:cu13-0.9.0'
docker pull "$DECODING_SERVER_IMAGE"
docker run -it --gpus all --network host --entrypoint bash "$DECODING_SERVER_IMAGE"

Inside the container, generate a configuration for a surface-code memory experiment and start the server:

memory-experiment-generator \
  --distance=3 --rounds=26 --basis=Z --decoder=pymatching \
  --error-rate=0.001 --output=memory.yaml

decoding_server --config=memory.yaml --transport=udp --port=50000 --timeout=3600

The server prints QEC_DECODING_SERVER_READY once its decoders are loaded and it is listening.

docs.title: Decoders are configuration
docs.text:
Each decoder the server hosts is an entry in a YAML file: its type, its parity-check and observable matrices, and any decoder-specific arguments. Here is the smallest example that ships with the server:

decoders:
  - id: 0
    type: pymatching
    block_size: 3
    syndrome_size: 3
    H_sparse: [0, -1, 1, -1, 2, -1]
    O_sparse: [0, -1, 1, -1, 2, -1]
    D_sparse: [0, -1, 1, -1, 2, -1]
    decoder_custom_args:
      error_rate_vec: [0.1, 0.1, 0.1]
      merge_strategy: smallest_weight

In production, you won't want to write these by hand. memory-experiment-generator builds them from a code distance, round count, basis, and error rate. The server can also export its own JSON schema with decoding_server --export-schema, so you can validate configs in CI before they reach the lab.

The container includes PyMatching, Chromobius for color codes, the NVIDIA Ising CNN predecoder paired with PyMatching through TensorRT, and the sliding-window and parallel-window decoders, which run another decoder inside each window. BP+OSD, Relay BP, and TCBP+JOBS all come from one GPU plugin, nv-qldpc-decoder: set the decoder's type to nv-qldpc-decoder and select the method in its decoder_custom_args. Decoders load as plugins, so you can bring your own decoder without rebuilding the server. Implement the C++ cudaq::qec::decoder interface, register it under a name, and build it as a shared library against the SDK headers and libraries in the image. Copy the .so into the image's decoder-plugins directory and set the decoder's type in the YAML to its registered name. The example plugin is a starting point, and the user guide walks through the build and deployment.

docs.title: A wire format any controller can speak
docs.text:
A controller talks to the server with four remote procedure calls. Each request is a 24-byte header followed by a tightly packed, little-endian payload. The header carries a magic number, the function ID, the payload length, a request ID, and a precision time protocol (PTP) timestamp that the server echoes back, so you can measure round trips on your own system.

Call What it does enqueue_syndromes Streams bit-packed syndromes to a decoder as rounds complete get_corrections Returns the corrections for the current shot get_logical_measurements Returns corrected logical measurement results reset_decoder Clears a decoder's state between shots

The full byte-level layout, including function IDs and status codes, is in MESSAGE_FORMAT.md. The transport underneath is a command-line choice. --transport=udp gets you running over standard IP networking on any NIC. --transport=cpu-roce uses RDMA over a ConnectX NIC with the Holoscan Sensor Bridge FPGA IP, the NVQLink network stack described in our cudaq-realtime launch post. And if your control system has its own network stack, you can load it as a shared library with --transport=/path/to/your_transport.so, with no changes to the server.

What runs where

In this release, the server dispatches every request from the host CPU. GPU decoders such as the Ising predecoder still run on the GPU; the host thread launches them. The real-time decoding interfaces are experimental and may change between releases.

docs.title: Test it before you have a QPU
docs.text:
You shouldn't need a physical QPU to find out whether your decoder configuration keeps up. The release includes a playback emulator that replays a timed schedule of decoder calls against a running server, over UDP or CPU RoCE, and records every response.

playback-emulator \
  --config=memory.yaml --schedule=memory_schedule.txt \
  --backend=udp --udp-endpoint=0:127.0.0.1:50000 --tick=1ms \
  --out=memory-result.csv

The same emulator is available from Python as cudaq_qec.playback. Because it drives the production server through the production wire format, a configuration that passes in playback is the configuration you deploy.

For timing, the streaming interleaved feed-forward latency (SIFL) demo measures how decode time per round changes as rounds arrive faster. That is the number that matters for feed-forward, and we encourage partners to report it on their own hosts. Playback and SIFL are functional and timing checks on your system; they are not a QPU feedback-latency guarantee.

docs.title: Compose decoders with task graphs
docs.text:
A single decoder per shot is fine for a short memory experiment. A real QEC workload streams thousands of rounds, mixes decoders, and needs answers before the stream ends. CUDA-Q QEC 0.9 introduces the decoding task graph to describe that work.

A task graph wires measurements through one or more decoding nodes to outputs, in Python or YAML. The same graph runs one-shot, batched, or streaming, offline in a notebook or live inside the Decoding Server. A chunked detector error model lets one configuration expand to any number of rounds, and streaming nodes accept rounds of different widths. For decoder ensembles racing a deadline, decoders now accept a cancellation token, so the graph can stop work it no longer needs.

docs.title: Block-parallel decoding
docs.text:
The most important node in this release is the parallel-window decoder, parallel_window. Following Skoric et al. 2023, it splits a long stream of rounds into two interleaved families of windows. Each A window corrects a fixed number of committed rounds, using buffer rounds of context on each side, and needs nothing from any other window. Each B window corrects the gap between two A windows once both neighbors have handed over the corrections at its edges.

A windows can all run at once, and each B window only waits on its two neighbors. That turns one long, serial decode into many short, parallel ones, so the work to finish any round is bounded by the window size rather than by the length of the stream.

import cudaq_qec as qec

# model: a chunked detector error model (DemChunksSpec) for your experiment.
# See the full parallel-window example for how to build it.
node = qec.TaskGraphNodeConfig()
node.id = "pw"
node.kind = "parallel_window"
node.dem = model
node.node_params = {
    "commit_rounds": 3,
    "buffer_rounds": 3,
    "gap_rounds": 9,
    "output": "corrections_and_logical",
}
node.max_in_flight = 4
node.decoder_type = "pymatching"
node.params = {"merge_strategy": "smallest_weight"}

options = qec.TaskGraphOptions()
options.async_streaming = True
graph = qec.DecodingTaskGraph.from_topology([node], options=options)

The decoder inside the windows is a parameter, so you can swap pymatching for any decoder that reports the faults it finds, not only the logical observables they flip.

docs.title: Keeping up with the QPU
docs.text:
How many windows you need in flight depends on how fast the QPU produces SERs and how long one window takes to decode. Each A window and the B window after it retire \(n_\text{com} + n_W\) SERs between them, where \(n_\text{com}\) is commit_rounds and \(n_W\) is gap_rounds, by default the size of an A window. Decoding that pair takes \(2\tau_W\), where \(\tau_W\) is the time to decode one window, including moving its syndromes in and its corrections out. With \(N_\text{par}\) windows decoding at once, the server retires \(N_\text{par}(n_\text{com} + n_W)\) SERs every \(2\tau_W\). The QPU produces one SER every \(\tau_\text{rd}\), which is 1 ms at 1 kHz and 1 µs at 1 MHz. The decoder keeps up if it retires SERs at least as fast as they arrive, which is the condition Skoric et al. 2023 derive:

\[ N_\text{par} \ge \frac{2\,\tau_W}{(n_\text{com} + n_W)\,\tau_\text{rd}} \]

In the code above, each pair of windows retires 3 + 9 = 12 SERs, and max_in_flight sets \(N_\text{par}\). The window decode time \(\tau_W\) depends on the decoder and the window size, not on the length of the stream. So the SER rate the server sustains grows in proportion to the number of windows in flight, while the reaction time is still set by the last window. It is the same arithmetic that put 57 SERs in flight on Willow, counted in windows instead of SERs.

Two examples show what this means in practice, one at each end of the SER range. Both run the parallel-window decoder in the Decoding Server on a GB200, with an FPGA streaming SERs from a distance-13 surface-code memory experiment (Figure 2). With commit_rounds and buffer_rounds equal to the code distance, each pair of windows retires 52 SERs.

In the first example, Relay BP runs inside each window on one GPU, and a window pair takes about 5.7 ms to decode. At 1 kHz, the condition above asks for about a tenth of a window, so one window in flight keeps up with room to spare. The server kept up at 3.2 kHz with one window and fell behind at 10 kHz, against a prediction of 9.1 kHz. That is more than three times the SER rate of a 1 kHz QPU.

In the second example, PyMatching runs inside each window on the CPU, and a window pair takes about 1.06 ms, so the server keeps up with faster QPUs by adding windows. The condition above predicts that 1, 2 and 4 windows in flight sustain about 49, 98 and 197 kHz. The server kept up at 54, 98 and 157 kHz and fell behind at 59, 117 and 225 kHz, so its limit lies between those rates. The prediction falls inside that range for 2 and 4 windows and is slightly conservative for 1.

Figure 2. SER rate the parallel-window decoder sustains in the Decoding Server versus windows in flight, with Relay BP or PyMatching inside each window, on a distance-13 surface-code memory experiment (Z basis, CNOT-only depolarizing noise, p = 0.001), with SERs streamed from an FPGA to a GB200. Each bar runs from the highest rate the server kept up with to the lowest rate where it fell behind. Open circles and the dashed line are the parallel-window condition, using the measured window decode time. Relay BP runs on one GPU; PyMatching used 4, 6 and 8 CPU cores for 1, 2 and 4 windows.

The parallel-window decoder also bounds the reaction time. A monolithic decoder can't finish until it has decoded the whole shot, so the time from the last SER to the result grows with the length of the shot. A window decoder has only the windows in the last packet of SERs left to decode when the shot ends. Figure 3 compares Relay BP run monolithically and inside the parallel-window decoder, at distances 3, 5 and 7. It shows the 99th-percentile time from the last packet leaving the FPGA to the server acknowledging that decoding is complete, with SERs sent in packets of 200 at an average of 10 to 12 kHz. Monolithic decoding reached 29 ms for a 10,000-SER shot at d=3, and over 100 ms for 8,000 SERs at d=5 and 4,000 SERs at d=7. The parallel-window decoder stayed under 6 ms at every shot length. At 1 kHz, a millisecond is one SER, so that is the difference between waiting 30 to 100 SERs at a feedforward event and waiting a few.

Figure 3. Time from the last packet of SERs to decode completion versus SERs per shot, for Relay BP decoding a surface-code memory experiment (Z basis, CNOT-only depolarizing noise, p = 0.001) monolithically and inside the parallel-window decoder. SERs were streamed from an FPGA to a GB200 in packets of 200, at 12,000 SERs/s for d=3 and 10,000 SERs/s for d=5 and d=7. Each point is the p99 over 20 shots, which is close to the slowest shot; lines are the median of three trials, and bands span all three.

docs.title: Introducing cudaq-realtime for programming the Logical QPU
docs.text:
Fault-tolerant quantum computing demands a tight classical–quantum feedback loop in which QEC decoding and autocalibration occur throughout QPU operation. Our new library, cudaq-realtime, builds on NVQLink by giving developers a runtime API for microsecond-latency callbacks between GPUs and quantum controllers.

In October 2025, we announced NVIDIA NVQLink, an open platform architecture that brings accelerated computing into the quantum stack.

At GTC 2026, NVQLink became publicly available through the release of the cudaq-realtime API in the NVIDIA CUDA-Q platform, allowing developers to write CUDA-Q code sending data back and forth between a quantum controller and GPUs. And partners are already taking advantage of this across the quantum computing ecosystem.

  • Dell has validated XE7745, XE9680, R7715 and R770 servers as Real-time Host platforms, reproducing NVQLink latencies under 4 µs.
  • Quantum Machines have integrated cudaq-realtime with their Open Acceleration Stack.
  • Qblox has adopted cudaq-realtime into their control electronics for OQC's full-stack quantum systems, enabling microsecond-level hybrid feedback loops.
  • SDT has deployed the first tightly-coupled hybrid quantum-classical data center in Korea, using SDT's controller and NVQLink to connect an Anyon Computing QPU to NVIDIA GPUs.
  • Atom Computing announced the successful integration of NVQLink into their proprietary control-systems stack.
  • IQM and Zurich Instruments are building a real-time QEC demonstrator combining an IQM 20-qubit QPU, the Zurich Instruments ZQCS Quantum Control System, and NVQLink.
  • Quantinuum has demonstrated demanding real-time QEC, performing correlated decoding of the Bring code on their Helios system with NVIDIA's GPU-accelerated BP+OSD decoder from the CUDA-Q QEC library.
  • Q-CTRL's software has obtained a 50x reduction in classical overhead and 5x speedup in overall wall-clock time by integrating NVQLink.
  • Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory used the architecture for the first integration of the open-source QubiC control system with NVIDIA DGX Spark and plans to perform AI-enhanced quantum control experiments, including readout classification and gate tuning.
  • Pacific Northwest National Laboratory is developing an open-source integration of the QICK FPGA control board with GH200 Grace Hopper via NVQLink, targeting GPU-accelerated QEC.
  • Elevate Quantum has launched Q-PAC, a commercially deployable open-architecture quantum system with QuantWare, Qblox, Q-CTRL, and Maybell components - including NVQLink-based GPU-cluster integration on the roadmap for 2026.

In this post we go under the hood to show how cudaq-realtime works, how it connects to real-time QEC decoding, what kind of latency you can expect across different host hardware, and how to reproduce these results on your own system.

docs.title: Why real-time compute matters for QPUs
docs.text:
QPUs require access to high-performance co-processing that can respond to function calls in real-time, faster than qubits decohere and keeping up with system drifts that cause gate fidelities to wander. The most stringent latency constraints come from QEC decoding, a massive, single-user inference task that has to happen right alongside the quantum processing with absolutely minimal latency. This task sets the clock speed of the QPU, so speeding it up is imperative.

A second critical workload is QPU calibration, in which measurements of physical properties of the QPU inform control parameters. Calibration happens during QPU bringup and continues during its online life while it performs work. With math acceleration and low latency data transfer, builders can apply adaptive measurement protocols and machine learning to make calibration orders of magnitude faster and more effective in reaching higher fidelities.

docs.title: The cudaq-realtime library
docs.text:
The core purpose of cudaq-realtime is to provide the ability for an FPGA to call functions on the GPU, getting the result back in microseconds. The FPGA sends a request, the GPU dispatches it to a registered handler, and the response goes back, all inside a persistent CUDA kernel with no host-side intervention on the hot path.

Figure 1. Architecture for dispatch from a persistent kernel to a registered handler in cudaq-realtime.

We separated the dispatch logic from the network transport, so cudaq-realtime can work with any physical link between an FPGA and a GPU. The NVQLink network stack is a reference implementation, built on RoCE via the Holoscan Sensor Bridge (HSB) FPGA IP and SDK, and a ConnectX NIC. But the network stack is pluggable via a bridge interface: any control system that can deliver packets to the GPU can serve as a cudaq-realtime transport by implementing this bridge. Quantum Machines, for example, have integrated their Open Acceleration Stack through the OPNIC, connecting their OPX1000 control system directly to CUDA-Q.

Higher-level libraries register their own handlers on top of this dispatch. For example, CUDA-Q QEC registers its decoders, so syndrome data from the FPGA goes straight to a GPU-accelerated decoder with no extra coordination.

docs.title: Kernel execution modes
docs.text: cudaq-realtime supports several kernel execution modes that trade off latency against flexibility.

docs.title: Three-kernel dispatch
docs.text:
The default mode uses three CUDA kernels that cooperate through GPU-visible ring buffers. One receives RDMA packets from the FPGA and writes them into a receive buffer, one polls that buffer, looks up the right handler, calls it, and writes the result to a transmit buffer, and one sends the response back to the FPGA.

The dispatch kernel never touches the network directly. It only sees ring buffer flags and data pointers, which means the same dispatch logic works no matter what transport bridge is underneath.

cudaq_ringbuffer_t ringbuffer{};
ringbuffer.rx_flags = rx_flags_dev;
ringbuffer.tx_flags = tx_flags_dev;
ringbuffer.rx_data  = rx_data_dev;
ringbuffer.tx_data  = tx_data_dev;
ringbuffer.rx_stride_sz = slot_size;
ringbuffer.tx_stride_sz = slot_size;

cudaq_dispatcher_set_ringbuffer(dispatcher, &ringbuffer);
cudaq_dispatcher_set_launch_fn(dispatcher,
    cudaq_launch_dispatch_kernel_regular);
cudaq_dispatcher_start(dispatcher);

docs.title: Unified kernel
docs.text:
The unified mode puts all three stages into one persistent kernel that handles RDMA receive, dispatch, and transmit directly through DOCA GPUNetIO. This cuts out the inter-kernel handoff and gives us the lowest dispatch latency, but it requires transport-specific code in the kernel.

cudaq_dispatcher_config_t config{};
config.kernel_type = CUDAQ_KERNEL_UNIFIED;

cudaq_dispatcher_set_unified_launch(dispatcher,
    hololink_launch_unified_dispatch, &transport_ctx);
cudaq_dispatcher_start(dispatcher);

docs.title: Transport-only forwarding kernel
docs.text: The forward mode bypasses cudaq-realtime dispatch entirely. A lightweight GPU kernel from the transport layer echoes each RDMA packet back through a symmetric ring buffer. This kernel type provides a clean baseline measurement of the network round trip alone.

docs.title: Cooperative kernel
docs.text:
For workloads that need grid-wide synchronization—multi-block belief propagation decoders, for example—we can launch the dispatch kernel in cooperative mode. After a grid.sync(), all threads across all blocks call the handler together, letting decoders spread work across the full GPU.

cudaq_dispatcher_config_t config{};
config.kernel_type = CUDAQ_KERNEL_COOPERATIVE;

cudaq_dispatcher_set_launch_fn(dispatcher,
    cudaq_launch_dispatch_kernel_cooperative);

docs.title: Benchmarking latency
docs.text:
We included a benchmarking function in cudaq-realtime to enable library users to understand the performance of NVQLink systems they have built or bought. This benchmark is intentionally simple, launching the dispatch kernel with a chosen kernel mode and measuring transit times using an integrated logic analyzer in the HSB IP.

By using the benchmark with different kernel modes, we can isolate different contributors to latency.

  • Forward mode measures buffer-to-buffer transport strictly, without any dispatch or function-call overhead.
  • Unified mode adds the latency of identifying a function and invoking the handler.
  • Three-kernel mode adds the latency of transfer among the RX, dispatch, and TX kernels.

We measured FPGA–GPU–FPGA round-trip latency using PTP timestamps on an RTX 6000 Blackwell Pro with ConnectX 7 NIC and a GB200 NVL4 with BlueField 3 NIC, in transport-only forward, unified, and three-kernel dispatch modes.

Figure 2. FPGA–GPU–FPGA round-trip latency across kernel types and host platforms, using the cudaq-realtime latency benchmark. Host Kernel Min (µs) Median (µs) Max (µs) RTX 6000 Blackwell Pro w/ ConnectX 7 (Oct '25) Forward 3.76 3.84 3.96 RTX 6000 Blackwell Pro w/ ConnectX 7 Forward 2.80 2.92 4.43 RTX 6000 Blackwell Pro w/ ConnectX 7 Unified 3.65 3.76 4.28 GB200 NVL4 w/ BlueField 3 Forward 5.14 5.31 7.22 GB200 NVL4 w/ BlueField 3 Unified 5.86 6.53 7.56 GB200 NVL4 w/ BlueField 3 Three-kernel 7.27 8.23 9.69

For reference, we quote our prior results from the October 2025 NVQLink paper. Since that measurement we have improved the underlying transport by roughly 0.9 µs, bringing the transport-only latency from 3.84 µs down to 2.92 µs.

Our GB200 NVL4 measurements were performed using a BlueField 3 SmartNIC on an experimental basis and are subject to further optimization.

docs.title: Real-time QEC decoding with cudaq-realtime and CUDA-Q QEC
docs.text:
cudaq-realtime is designed to be a building block. CUDA-Q QEC uses it by registering decoders as RPC handlers in the dispatch kernel, so that syndrome data arriving from the FPGA is routed directly to the right GPU-accelerated decoder.

The real-time QEC workflow starts with a detector error model (DEM) that captures the error characteristics of the device.

import cudaq
import cudaq_qec as qec

cudaq.set_target("stim")
noise = cudaq.NoiseModel()
noise.add_all_qubit_channel("x", cudaq.Depolarization2(0.01), 1)
dem = qec.z_dem_from_memory_circuit(code, qec.operation.prep0, 3, noise)

From the DEM, you configure a decoder and save the configuration. Before running circuits, CUDA-Q QEC loads the config, sets up the parity check matrix, and registers the decoder with the runtime.

config = qec.decoder_config()
config.id = 0
config.type = "nv-qldpc-decoder"
config.block_size = dem.detector_error_matrix.shape[1]
config.syndrome_size = dem.detector_error_matrix.shape[0]
config.H_sparse = qec.pcm_to_sparse_vec(dem.detector_error_matrix)
config.O_sparse = qec.pcm_to_sparse_vec(dem.observables_flips_matrix)
# ... set D_sparse and decoder-specific params from DEM ...

multi_config = qec.multi_decoder_config()
multi_config.decoders = [config]

with open("config.yaml", 'w') as f:
    f.write(multi_config.to_yaml_str())

qec.configure_decoders_from_file("config.yaml")

At runtime, syndrome measurements flow to the decoder and corrections come back. The same kernel code works in simulation and on physical hardware—the runtime routes calls to the appropriate backend.

import cudaq
import cudaq_qec as qec
from cudaq_qec import patch

@cudaq.kernel
def qec_circuit() -> int:
    qec.reset_decoder(0)

    data = cudaq.qvector(3)
    ancz = cudaq.qvector(2)
    ancx = cudaq.qvector(0)
    logical = patch(data, ancx, ancz)

    prep0(logical)

    for _ in range(3):
        syndromes = measure_stabilizers(logical)
        qec.enqueue_syndromes(0, syndromes, 0)

    corrections = qec.get_corrections(0, 1, False)
    if corrections[0]:
        for i in range(3):
            x(data[i])

    return cudaq.to_integer(mz(data))

The enqueue_syndromes call is asynchronous. The QPU keeps running while the GPU decodes, and only blocks when get_corrections is called. This pipelining keeps the QPU productive during the decode window.

CUDA-Q QEC ships with several decoder algorithms that all work through this interface: GPU-accelerated Relay-BP for qLDPC codes, TensorRT-based AI decoders, and sliding window decoders for tight latency budgets. The CUDA-Q QEC documentation and real-time decoding examples have the full details.

docs.title: Get started
docs.text:
The cudaq-realtime library is available today in the realtime directory of the CUDA-Q repository. Full documentation, including API reference and tutorials, is at the cudaq-realtime docs. The build produces libcudaq-realtime.so and a self-extracting installer. You can install it on any CUDA-capable system with a compatible network interface to FPGA. Connect an FPGA via RoCE, or use the built-in emulator if you do not have one yet, and run the latency benchmark.

cd realtime/unittests/utils

# Transport-only forward (FPGA echo, no dispatch)
./hololink_test.sh --forward

# CUDA-Q unified kernel (lowest CUDA-Q latency)
./hololink_test.sh --unified

# CUDA-Q three-kernel (default, transport-agnostic)
./hololink_test.sh

# Use --emulate for development without an FPGA
./hololink_test.sh --emulate

The benchmark writes ptp_latency.csv with per-sample round-trip timestamps. Compare your numbers to the characterization in the NVQLink paper.

For a minimal working example, see realtime/examples/gpu_dispatch/, which registers a handler and processes requests through the dispatch kernel.

Whether you are building QPUs, developing decoders, or bringing GPU acceleration into your quantum lab, cudaq-realtime is the starting point for real-time programming on NVQLink.
